title: Sausage Roll
subtitle: Seasoned pork mince in flaky puff pastry, baked until golden
excerpt: A British sausage roll is a tube of seasoned pork mince enclosed in puff pastry and baked until the pastry is shatteringly flaky and the meat inside is juicy. The trick is in the seasoning: sage, mustard, and a little nutmeg lift the pork above what comes out of a sausage skin. Homemade sausage rolls are better than any you can buy.
sourceNotes: Sausage rolls have been a fixture of British baking and party food since at least the early nineteenth century. They appear in Victorian cookbooks as a standard light pastry alongside vol-au-vents and patties.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze unbaked on a tray, then transfer to a bag. Bake from frozen at 180°C fan for 35 minutes until cooked through.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a large batch and freeze most unbaked. Pull out as many as you need and bake from frozen.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Assemble and refrigerate up to 24 hours before baking.

content.text: Sausage rolls depend on three things: well-seasoned meat, cold pastry, and a hot oven. The meat should not be too lean: a little fat keeps it juicy during baking. The pastry should go from the fridge into the oven without getting warm. And the oven should be hot enough to puff and colour the pastry quickly, before the fat in the meat has time to turn the base soggy.

items.prepNote: 1 for the filling, 1 beaten for glaze

content.text: Grated onion (not chopped) disappears into the meat without creating texture. A small amount of flour or fine breadcrumbs binds the filling and absorbs any released juices during baking.

Combine {{pork-mince}} of pork mince with the grated onion, sage, {{english-mustard}} of English mustard, {{plain-flour}} of flour, and 1 beaten egg. Season generously with salt and pepper. Mix well until combined. Fry a small piece in a pan to taste for seasoning, and adjust.

Roll the puff pastry into a rectangle about 40 x 30 cm if not already in that shape. Cut in half lengthways so you have two long strips. Divide the filling in half. Roll each portion of filling into a long sausage and place along the centre of each pastry strip.

Brush one long edge of each pastry strip with beaten egg. Roll the pastry over the filling, pressing the egg-brushed edge down firmly to seal. Turn seam side down. Brush the tops with beaten egg and score with a fork or knife. Chill for 15 minutes.
Heat the oven to 200°C fan. Cut each log into 6 pieces. Place on a lined baking tray. Bake for 22 to 25 minutes until the pastry is deeply golden and the filling is cooked through.

items.symptom: The pastry is soggy on the bottom
items.cause: The meat released too much fat during baking.
items.fix: Use meat with about 20% fat, not more. The flour or breadcrumbs in the filling also help absorb excess juices. Bake on a dark metal tray on the middle shelf.

items.symptom: The filling cracks and spills out
items.cause: The filling was packed too tight or the pastry seal was too thin.
items.fix: Leave a slight gap in the filling so the pastry can shrink as it cooks. Make sure the seal is a solid double fold, not just a pressed edge.

items.cause: Pork mince on its own is mild; it needs confident seasoning.
items.fix: Season the filling more aggressively than feels comfortable before baking, as flavour mutes slightly when cooked. The test fry in the pan is the best check.

items.symptom: The pastry puffs but does not colour
items.cause: The egg wash was too thin, or the oven was not fully preheated.
items.fix: Brush generously with beaten egg (not just the yolk) and bake in a fully preheated oven. A pale sausage roll needs 5 more minutes.

content.text: The sausage roll is one of the most enduring items in British baking. It appears at every scale, from birthday parties to bar snacks. A national bakery chain built a business on this format. The original pork and sage version in flaky puff pastry remains the benchmark. Homemade is always better.
